docs.title: Loom
docs.text: A proof-of-concept virtual machine for unordered, streaming execution of data-parallel SPMD programs.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Loom is an experimental software framework exploring an alternative approach to data-parallel execution.

It implements an abstract execution machine for Single Program Multiple Data (SPMD) programs, using dynamic instance regrouping and unordered scheduling to improve execution efficiency on workloads with irregular control flow and divergent execution paths.

The project explores a programming and execution model that can target different parallel processing architectures, including CPU SIMD and GPU SIMT hardware.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Unordered execution: Program instances are scheduled dynamically rather than following a globally synchronized execution order.
  • Dynamic regrouping: Instances executing the same basic block are grouped together to improve execution coherence.
  • Streaming execution: Work progresses through the execution system without requiring global ordering of independent instances.
  • Persistent execution state: Virtual registers preserve per-instance state across scheduling cycles.
  • Multiple backends: The abstract machine can be implemented on different hardware architectures.
  • Inspectable execution: Development tools provide facilities for inspecting and debugging execution behavior.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
To build all benchmarks and demo you need:

  • GNU/Linux distribution
  • 32Gb RAM required (explanation)

docs.title: Build with nix
docs.text:
The easiest way to build is to use nix package manager.

Just cd to source directory and run nix build.

Apart from default build target there are complete and minimal ones.

docs.title: Build in a generic linux distro
docs.text: Even if you don't run NixOS or don't have nix installed you still can build everything with CMake.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
• CMake
  • LLVM Clang 19 or newer
  • LLVM Libc++ 19 or newer
  • libfmt 9 or newer
  • glfw3
  • range-v3
  • fast_float
  • hwloc

The last four can be downloaded by cmake.

./build.sh -b -demo -l to build benchmarks and demo, add -f if you're too lazy to install dependencies with your distro package manager. See ./build.sh -h for more options.

If you're going to build manually with CMake ensure the stack size is unlocked: ulimit -s unlimited. Otherwise, the build of path-tracing benchmarks and demo will fail with stack overflow error.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
To run all benchmarks you need CPU with at least AVX support, but the best results give AVX-512 processors (not only because of SIMD width).

Run all benchmarks: src/scripts/benchmark all <dir_with_binaries> <dir_with_benchmark_results>.

For example, nix users have <dir_with_binaries> to be result/bin/.

If you don't want to run all benchmarks (it can take quite a while), the other options for benchmarks are light and render. render benchmarks still take a lot of time.

To inspect results of path tracing benchmarks there is a quick'n'dirty script in src/scripts/report.py.

Invoke it with one argument:

report.py <dir_with_benchmark_results>

docs.title: Path-tracing demo
docs.text: The interactive demo executable is called loom_pt_demo. Invoke with -h to see available options.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The project implements an abstract execution machine for data-parallel SPMD programs.

Unlike conventional SIMD and SIMT execution models, where groups of program instances typically advance through execution in a coordinated manner, this machine uses dynamic scheduling and regrouping based on the current execution state of individual instances.

The primary objective is to reduce the impact of control-flow divergence while maintaining a relatively simple and portable execution model.

docs.title: SPMD Programming
docs.text:
A program is defined once and executed by multiple independent instances. Each instance maintains its own execution state and progresses through the same program according to its input data and control flow.

Instances do not require a globally synchronized execution order.

docs.title: Abstract Machine
docs.text:
The abstract machine operates on a collection of execution instances, each maintaining:

  • A set of virtual registers representing persistent program state.
  • A program counter identifying the next basic block to execute.
  • Input and output values defining the instance's interaction with the surrounding system.

The machine executes instructions associated with the current basic block and updates the execution state of each instance.

docs.title: Basic Blocks and Control Flow
docs.text:
Programs are represented as control-flow graphs composed of basic blocks.

Each basic block contains a sequence of instructions and terminates with a control-flow operation that determines the next block pointer.

The block pointer is the primary scheduling key used to identify instances that can execute the same basic block together.

docs.title: Dynamic Grouping
docs.text:
At scheduling boundaries, execution instances are grouped according to their block pointers.

Instances sharing the same block pointer can execute the corresponding basic block together, improving execution coherence.

docs.title: Unordered Execution
docs.text:
The execution system does not maintain the original ordering of independent instances.

This removes the need to reconstruct a global execution order after regrouping and allows instances to progress according to their individual execution requirements.

docs.title: Streaming Execution
docs.text:
The machine processes instances incrementally. Completed or otherwise eligible instances can exchange execution slots with newly available work, allowing the system to maintain throughput without requiring all instances to complete together.

docs.title: Hardware Mapping
docs.text: The abstract machine is designed to support multiple implementation strategies.

docs.title: CPU SIMD
docs.text: On CPUs, groups of instances can be mapped to fixed-width SIMD execution units. Predication and vector instruction selection can be used to handle differences between individual instance states.

docs.title: GPU SIMT
docs.text: On GPUs, the execution model can be mapped to hardware execution groups and scheduling units. Dynamic regrouping provides an alternative to relying exclusively on hardware-managed divergence and reconvergence.

docs.title: Heterogeneous Execution
docs.text: The abstract execution model is not inherently tied to a specific hardware architecture. Different backends can implement the same programming semantics while exploiting their respective hardware capabilities.

docs.title: Implementation Architecture
docs.text:
The implementation is organized around several major components:

  • Program representation: Defines the instruction set, basic blocks and control-flow relationships.
  • Execution memory: Stores persistent execution state for active instances.
  • Scheduler: Selects and groups instances for execution.
  • Execution backend: Implements instruction execution on the target hardware.
  • Input/output handling: Provides interfaces for supplying work and collecting results.
  • Inspection and debugging: Exposes execution state and scheduling behavior for development and analysis.
